title: EIP-8450: Post-Quantum Validator Key Registry
description: Register dormant hash-based consensus keys for every validator ahead of the post-quantum signature switch
author: Thomas Coratger (@tcoratger), Kevaundray Wedderburn (@kevaundray), Tom Wambsgans (@TomWambsgans), Justin Drake (@JustinDrake)
bodyPreview: ## Abstract This EIP adds a post-quantum public key registry to the beacon state. Each validator registers one hash-based public key, bound to its existing validator index: a leanXMSS key, used for every message the validator signs once duties switch to it. The leanXMSS key is a two-layer tree: a top tree of `2**16` one-time keys, each of which certifies a bottom tree of `2**16` one-time keys, for a lifetime of `2**32` leaf indices. No step of key generation handles more than `2**16` one-time keys. Every signature carries its leaf index, and the signer chooses how leaf indices are allocated to messages, provided no leaf index signs two different messages. All hashing uses Keccak-256. Registration is a new beacon block operation carrying the public key and a proof of possession under it. It is authorized either by the validator's current BLS signing key (register-only) or by the validator's withdrawal address through a new [EIP-7685](./eip-7685.md) request (register or replace). The registered keys are dormant: no duty is authenticated with them in this fork. A later fork switches duties to them. For that fork, the registry provides the fraction of stake with registered keys, and a post-quantum public key for every registered validator. ## Motivation Every consensus-layer signature today is a BLS12-381 signature: attestations, block proposals, RANDAO reveals, aggregation selection proofs, sync committee messages, payload attestations, inclusion lists, proposer preferences, voluntary exits, and the deposit proof of possession. BLS relies on the hardness of discrete logarithms in pairing-friendly groups, which Shor's algorithm breaks. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) recovers a validator's secret key from its public key, and every validator's public key is in the beacon state. BLS therefore has to be replaced, and this EIP splits the replacement into two forks. Generating a post-quantum key involves the validator's secret key material, requires new tooling, and, for staking pools, requires coordination between node operators and stake owners. If this work happens at the fork that switches the signature scheme, the number of ready validators is only known at that fork. If a CRQC appears before the switch, no post-quantum key exists to fall back on, and any message signed with BLS after that point may be forged. A separate registry fork has the following benefits: - **Preparation.** Validators generate and register keys, with tooling tested on mainnet, while BLS remains the only scheme used for duties. - **A readiness signal.** The fraction of stake with registered keys can be read from the state, so the switch can be scheduled against an observed threshold. - **A recovery anchor.** Keys registered while BLS is secure are authentic. If BLS breaks before the switch, the chain can move to the registered keys without relying on any BLS signature made after the break. - **Early implementation.** Consensus clients start manipulating the hash function, the verifier, and the containers of the post-quantum scheme before any duty depends on them, because every registration carries a proof of possession that clients verify. Each validator registers one leanXMSS key for all of its messages. The [Rationale](#one-key-for-all-duties) explains this choice and the two ways a signer can allocate leaf indices. ## Specification The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119) and [RFC 8174](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8174). The consensus-layer changes apply to the consensus specifications (`ethereum/consensus-specs`) on top of Heze. The execution-layer changes apply on top of the execution-layer fork paired with it. The fork that activates this EIP is assigned by the relevant meta EIP. Functions and constants not defined here keep their meaning from those specifications. ### Cryptographic primitives #### Hash function All post-quantum hashing in this EIP uses `keccak256`, the Keccak-256 hash function of the execution layer, in the cell encoding of leanVM. The input is split into 128-byte chunks, the last one possibly shorter, and consecutive chunks are joined by the 8 bytes `CELL_GAP`. Inputs of at most 128 bytes are therefore hashed unchanged. On longer inputs, each 136-byte Keccak-256 block carries 128 input bytes, which keeps the 16-byte cells of the leanVM verifier aligned. ```python CELL_GAP = bytes(7) + b"\x80" def lean_hash(data: bytes) -> Bytes32: """ Hash bytes with Keccak-256 in the cell encoding. The input is cut into 128-byte chunks. An 8-byte gap separates consecutive chunks. Each 136-byte Keccak block then holds exactly 128 input bytes. """ # Cut into 128-byte chunks. # An empty input is a single empty chunk. chunks = [data[i:i + 128] for i in range(0, len(data), 128)] or [b""] # Join with the gap and hash. # An input of at most 128 bytes is hashed unchanged. return keccak256(CELL_GAP.join(chunks)) def th(public_param: Hash16, address: bytes, message: bytes) -> Hash16: """ Hash one call of a key. The public parameter separates keys. The address separates the calls within a key. The output keeps the first 16 bytes of the hash. """ # Input layout: public parameter (16), address (16), message. return Hash16(lean_hash(bytes(public_param) + address + message)[:16]) ``` `public_param` is a 16-byte per-key public parameter. The address names the hash call within the key: ```python # Types of the hash calls a verifier makes. ADDRESS_CHAIN = 1 ADDRESS_LEAF = 2 ADDRESS_NODE = 3 ADDRESS_MESSAGE = 12 def xmss_address(kind: int, step: int, layer: int, high: int, low: int) -> bytes: """ Build the 16-byte address of one hash call. bytes 0..4 one-time key or node index bytes 4..7 tree level, with the layer in the top bit byte 7 call type + 32 * chain step bytes 8..16 zero All integers
